source: Taatgen, Huss, Dickison, Anderson (2008) The acquisition of robust and flexible cognitive skills, JEP:General 137(3) - Exp 1
finding: People learned flight-management-system procedures from either plain step lists or 'context' instructions that state pre- and postconditions. Context instructions gave higher accuracy and faster solutions, mostly on hard problems that the literal steps did not cover.
numbers: N=31 (list vs context). Accuracy 77.0% list vs 91.1% context, F(1,29)=7.09, p=.014. Hard problems 70.4% vs 89.9%, t(17.9)=2.6, p=.018; easy 90.4% vs 93.8%, n.s. Solution time 28.7 s vs 24.8 s, F(1,29)=5.85, p=.022.
limits: One simulated task (Boeing 777 FMS), CMU students, about 1 hr. Effect confined to non-literal problems.
agent_relevance: Store a lesson with its trigger condition and expected outcome, not as a bare step list. That let compiled rules survive novel cases.

source: Taatgen, Huss, Dickison, Anderson (2008) The acquisition of robust and flexible cognitive skills, JEP:General 137(3) - Exp 2 (replication with partial and erroneous states)
finding: Replicated Exp 1 with new problem types: half-completed procedures, some with an error. The model predicted these before the data came in. Context advantage held but was weaker.
numbers: N=40. Accuracy 78.8% list vs 89.0% context, F(1,38)=4.5, p=.040. Time 27.2 s vs 23.0 s, F(1,38)=3.60, p=.066 (marginal). Prediction fits R2 .66 to .75 for accuracy.
limits: Effect for error-recovery problems only approached significance. Time effect marginal.
agent_relevance: Recovery from a wrong or half-done state depends on the lesson being state-conditional.

source: Taatgen, Huss, Dickison, Anderson (2008) The acquisition of robust and flexible cognitive skills, JEP:General 137(3) - Exp 3 (four instruction types)
finding: Third experiment with fully randomised order and four conditions. Context instructions still helped, but the effect shrank and the condition-by-difficulty interaction disappeared. An extended list gave no gain over a simple list. A graphic mental-model version gave no extra gain.
numbers: N=100 (25 per condition). Block effect on log time F(1,96)=286.7. Some contrasts were small and not significant, e.g. 26.0 s vs 26.9 s, t(44.1)=0.80, p>.10, and 77.6% vs 82.1%, p>.10. Model predicted 21.8 s and 90.9% for context, 28.6 s and 80.8% for lists; people were less accurate than predicted. Context model fit for accuracy fell to R2=.44.
limits: Authors say the difference is 'smaller in Experiment 3'. Randomised order removed the difficulty interaction, so part of the earlier picture may come from blocked order.
agent_relevance: The benefit of a richer format is real but modest once practice order is mixed. Do not expect big wins from reformatting alone.

source: Taatgen, Huss, Dickison, Anderson (2008) The acquisition of robust and flexible cognitive skills, JEP:General 137(3) - model fit and parameters
finding: The ACT-R model starts from declarative instructions. Production compilation turns them into task rules. Three parameters were fitted on Exp 1 only, then used to predict Exp 2 and 3. Compiled rules start with very low utility, so they win only after repeated use.
numbers: Exp 1 fit: list accuracy RMSE 0.078; context accuracy R2=0.82, RMSE 0.043; list time R2=0.70, RMSE 10.2; context time R2=0.52, RMSE 9.1. Each operator had a 25% chance of being forgotten in the model.
limits: Time fits are weaker than accuracy fits. One strategy modelled, although people vary.
agent_relevance: A new routine should not replace its parent lesson at once. It should earn selection by repeated success.

source: Taatgen (2005) Modeling parallelization and flexibility improvements in skill acquisition, Cognitive Science 29(3) - Schumacher et al. 2001 dual-task fit
finding: Production compilation plus a weak hierarchy of instructions reproduced how people reach perfect time-sharing in dual tasks. Dual-task costs on Day 2 vanished by Day 5, in both the data and the model.
numbers: Exp 1 of Schumacher et al.: 45-trial pure blocks, 48-trial mixed blocks (18 dual). A new rule saves 100 ms (one rule, one retrieval); it starts to build up around 100 experiences, peaks near 150 and then wins about 95% of the time. Residual parent selection under 1%.
limits: Fit shown as figures, not summary statistics. Incompatible-mapping cost was set by hand because the model could not explain it.
agent_relevance: Gains from merging steps accrue slowly (about a hundred uses), so a routine library needs a promotion threshold based on use counts.

source: Taatgen (2005) Modeling parallelization and flexibility improvements in skill acquisition, Cognitive Science 29(3) - individual differences in dual-task cost
finding: Differences in residual dual-task cost were explained by one parameter: how long the production that starts the motor response takes. Fast and slow participants were reproduced by changing it.
numbers: 5 of 11 participants had almost no dual-task cost at the end; they were also the fastest. Setting the rule time to 0.15 s reproduced them; 0.35 s reproduced the 4 participants with large costs (default 0.2 s).
limits: Author says 'more solid evidence is needed'. Post-hoc parameter fit on 11 people, not a test.
agent_relevance: Speed of a compiled routine depends on its slowest step, not on its length.

source: Taatgen (2005) Modeling parallelization and flexibility improvements in skill acquisition, Cognitive Science 29(3) - comparison with rival learning accounts
finding: Reviews rivals. ACT* had four rule-learning mechanisms (proceduralization, composition, specialization, generalization) that produced rules too fast to evaluate. Soar chunking learns from impasse traces. Logan's instance theory has retrieval racing a general algorithm. ACT-R keeps one mechanism, compilation.
numbers: No new experimental numbers; qualitative comparison.
limits: Second-hand description of Logan and Newell; author is an advocate of ACT-R. No experiment is given that separates the accounts.
agent_relevance: Links to the Soar chunking page in this series (C02/03). Lesson-to-routine is closer to compilation (from declarative) than chunking (from impasse).

source: Taatgen and Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition, Human Factors 45(1)
finding: One ACT-R model learned the Kanfer-Ackerman air traffic controller task from instructions via compilation, at three levels: whole task, unit tasks, keystrokes. It used default parameters.
numbers: Data from Ackerman and Kanfer (1994) Study 2: 65 undergraduates, 18 trials of 10 min; model compared on trials 1-10. Planes landed r2=.97 over 10 trials; land unit task r2=.98; other unit task fits r2=.87 to .91.
limits: Model beat people in early trials because it started with all declarative knowledge and screen locations. It used one strategy while people use several. Strategy discovery was not modelled.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that hands the agent complete instructions will overstate early-trial skill compared with a learner; discovery of the task knowledge itself is the unmodelled part.

source: Taatgen and Lee (2003) - strategy shift as a by-product
finding: As the model got faster it moved from a sequential strategy (land one plane, then fetch the next) to an opportunistic strategy (keep the holding level full). No strategy rule was added; speed alone caused it.
numbers: Matches John and Lallement (1997) strategy shift qualitatively. No effect size.
limits: Explanation is the model's own; not tested by manipulating speed in people.
agent_relevance: Speed-ups from compiled routines can change which strategy pays off. Re-check strategy choice after routines form.

source: Taatgen (2002) A model of individual differences in skill acquisition (as described in Taatgen and Lee 2003)
finding: Earlier model varied working memory capacity, speed of production compilation and psychomotor speed. It reproduced the pattern of correlations Ackerman (1988) found between abilities and performance.
numbers: No numbers in the second-hand text.
limits: Original not opened. The later model approximated the task interaction only.
agent_relevance: Learning speed is a dimension separate from capacity. For an agent, compile rate is a tunable setting.

source: Taatgen and Anderson (2002) Why do children learn to say 'broke'? Cognition 86(2)
finding: A compilation model produced U-shaped learning of English past tense without feedback and without a built-in vocabulary change. Retrieval of stored forms competes with a rule built from analogy and compilation.
numbers: Model overregularisation correlated with parent verb frequency at -0.59; Marcus (1996) found -0.34 in child data. Corpus of 478 verbs (89 irregular, 389 regular). Similar behaviour in majority-default, minority-default and no-input variants.
limits: Model uses very limited representations and analogy. Authors say it cannot handle verbs such as 'want' fully. Correlation is higher than in children, which they blame on noisy frequency estimates.
agent_relevance: A compiled rule can over-apply to exceptions and fade only as exceptions are memorised. Expect a dip before improvement when a routine is first promoted.

source: Taatgen and Anderson (2002) - connectionist rivals criticised
finding: Network models need feedback, depend on vocabulary growth or input frequency schedules, and some show a U-shape in regular verbs too, which children do not show. These are the points where the compilation model claims an edge.
numbers: Marcus et al. (1992): dips in irregulars coincide with gains in regulars. Plunkett and Marchman (1993) needed a vocabulary jump near 100 verbs. Plunkett and Juola: generalisation absent unless regulars exceed 50%.
limits: Written in 2002; later connectionist work not covered. Author is a party to the dispute.
agent_relevance: The cleanest argument for compilation over weights is that no external feedback signal is required.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere, Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R
finding: States the mechanism. Two rules that fire in sequence merge into one. If the first asks declarative memory and the second uses the answer, the retrieved chunk is baked into the new rule and the retrieval disappears. A merge is blocked when both rules need the same buffer (for example the same hand).
numbers: Examples: instruction plus key press compiled into one 'land plane, push enter' rule; a retrieved past case (DC10, dry runway) compiled into a case rule.
limits: Describes ACT-R 5.0. Later versions changed details.
agent_relevance: Baking a retrieved fact into a rule is the analogue of turning a stored lesson into a fixed routine. The cost: the rule only holds for that retrieved case.

source: Taatgen (2000) Learning rules and productions, Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science
finding: Survey of rule learning from examples (version spaces, generalisation and specialisation). Notes version-space methods handle noise and disjunction badly and that each step raises the number of candidate rules.
numbers: No experimental numbers.
limits: Pre-LLM overview. Not evidence on compilation itself.
agent_relevance: Background: inducing rules from many examples is a separate problem from compiling known steps.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: An LLM agent stores verified code programs as a skill library and reuses them. This is the closest LLM analogue of turning lessons into routines. The library mattered most later in a run and on unseen tasks, not early.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x baselines. Tech tree: wooden 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x faster; only agent to reach diamond (1 of 3 runs, 102 iterations). Iron tool 21 +/-7 with library vs 29 +/-11 without; wooden 6 vs 7, stone 11 vs 9. Unseen tasks (50-iteration cap): diamond pickaxe 19 +/-3 (3/3) vs 36 (2/3) without library; golden sword 18 +/-7 vs 30 +/-9; lava bucket 21 +/-5 vs 27 +/-9; compass 18 +/-2 vs 26 +/-3. AutoGPT given the library: 1/3, 1/3, 0/3, 2/3.
limits: Three runs per cell. One game, GPT-4. Library alone is not enough: random curriculum -93% items, no self-verification -73%.
agent_relevance: Library helps late and on transfer but not early. Gate entries by verification; self-verification was the largest ablation.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agents induce reusable workflows from past trajectories and keep them in memory. Gains on WebArena and Mind2Web, with fewer steps.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): 35.5% overall success, +12.0 points absolute and 51.1% relative over BrowserGym; 7.6% relative above SteP, which uses human-written workflows. About 2.0 fewer steps per example than BrowserGym and 40.8 fewer than AutoEval. Mind2Web cross-task step success +24.6% relative.
limits: Adding workflows as callable actions added only 1.3 step-success points and the same overall score; agents called them in just 18.5% of tasks. WebArena templates overlap, so some gain is in-template; a cross-template subset is reported separately.
agent_relevance: Agents under-use new routines even when available. A routine library needs explicit prompting to be used.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Memp: exploring agent procedural memory
finding: Builds procedural memory from past trajectories at three granularities: script, raw trajectory, and 'proceduralization' (both). Cites procedural memory as silently compiling skills. Combined form gave the largest gains on ALFWorld.
numbers: ALFWorld dev, GPT-4o: no memory 39.28, script 66.67, trajectory 67.17, proceduralization 87.14; test 42.14, 56.43, 74.29, 77.86; steps 23.76 down to 15.01. Claude-3.5-sonnet dev 39.20 to 82.50. Qwen2.5-72b dev 44.91 to 85.71. TravelPlanner hard-constraint score for GPT-4o: 12.88 no memory, script 5.50, proceduralization 9.76 (both worse). Procedural memory built by GPT-4o and given to a smaller model raised completion by 5% and cut 1.6 steps.
limits: Hard-constraint score on TravelPlanner got worse with memory for GPT-4o while commonsense score rose. Retrieving too many memories lowered performance. Dev sets are small.
agent_relevance: Lesson-to-routine can help one metric and hurt another. Cap how many routines are retrieved. Routines from a strong model carry to a weaker one.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent extracts natural-language insights from success and failure pairs and also retrieves past trajectories. Insights help knowledge tasks; retrieved trajectories help action tasks.
numbers: Restricting to insights only or retrieval only: HotpotQA 36% / 31%, ALFWorld 50% / 55%. ALFWorld 'put' success 61 (insights) / 73 (retrieval) / 83 (full). 'heat' was 87 / 74 / 43, so the full method was worse on that type.
limits: Per-type cells are small and noisy. Some task types did worse with the full method.
agent_relevance: Keep both an abstract rule and concrete worked cases; they cover different task types.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Self-supervised 'compile' of slow reasoning into direct answers by fine-tuning. Works for some prompts and fails for chain-of-thought maths, the clearest boundary condition found for compiling.
numbers: Last-letter task: base 30.0%, 2-step RaR 44.5%, distilled 98.0%. Coin flip: 56.1% base, 77.2% 2-step RaR, 75.69% distilled. TriviaQA S2A bias test: 51.6% base, 76.0% S2A, 81.3% distilled with 56 vs 147 tokens. GSM8k: CoT zero-shot 36.39% (k=1) vs distilled CoT 7.13%, near the 7.58 to 9.40% of direct answering.
limits: Needs unlabeled data and consistency filtering. This is fine-tuning, not scaffolding. Failure is on multi-step arithmetic that needs intermediate tokens.
agent_relevance: Not every skill folds into a routine. Keep explicit steps for multi-step calculation; compile only stable pattern tasks.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large language models as tool makers (LATM)
finding: A strong model writes a reusable Python tool once; a cheap model then uses it. Cost is spread over many uses, like a compiled rule that skips retrieval. Gains vanish when the user model is already strong.
numbers: GPT-3.5 Turbo CoT to LATM: logical deduction 66.4 to 79.7; tracking shuffled objects 61.6 to 99.6; Dyck 20.4 to 92.2; word sorting 59.2 to 98.3; Chinese remainder 0.0 to 100.0; schedule meeting 18.9 to 100.0. GPT-4 user, CoT to LATM: logical deduction 88.8 to 86.6; Dyck 63.6 to 87.5.
limits: Six tasks with regular structure, no free-form tasks. Tool maker is the costly model. Column order read from the table text.
agent_relevance: A compiled tool pays off when the task is regular and the user model is weak.

source: Su et al. (2025) Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking by randomized reasoning traces
finding: Trains one model on search traces randomly truncated so it can run fast (no trace), slow (full trace) or pick its own mode. Partial compilation of a search routine.
numbers: Mazes 30x30: slow mode 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% optimal vs 30% for a solution-only model; auto mode 96.6% optimal with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Mazes and Sokoban only; small models trained from scratch on A* traces, not a general LLM scaffold.
agent_relevance: Mixed training on full and cut traces beats answer-only training. Keep a slow mode available.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: web agents can self-improve by discovering and honing skills
finding: Agent explores sites, writes reusable API-like skills, practises them, and keeps the ones that pass. Skills built by a strong agent lifted weaker agents.
numbers: Abstract: relative success gain 31.8% on WebArena and 39.8% on real-world sites; up to 54.3% for weaker agents using skills from strong ones. Baseline 25% to 38% after 160 iterations in one experiment. The results text also quotes 39.8% average on WebArena with GPT-4o, so check which condition before citing.
limits: Different parts of the paper give different headline percentages. Sites change and skills go stale.
agent_relevance: Practise and verify before keeping a routine. A skill from a strong model transfers down.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA)
finding: Framework paper mapping LLM agents onto Soar and ACT-R ideas. Treats procedural memory as production rules and code in the agent; notes Soar can write new productions.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Conceptual only. Gives no test of compilation.
agent_relevance: Use its vocabulary to place the lesson-to-routine step inside the agent's memory design.

source: Anderson (1982) Acquisition of cognitive skill; Anderson (1987) Skill acquisition: compilation of weak-method problem solutions (not opened; seen in a Semantic Scholar listing)
finding: Original theory that compilation turns weak-method problem solving into task rules. Parent of Taatgen's account.
numbers: Citation counts only: 3936 (1982), 689 (1987).
limits: Not read. Taatgen 2005 says the ACT* version had four mechanisms.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Logan (1988) Toward an instance theory of automatization (not opened)
finding: Rival account: practice speeds up because stored instances race the general algorithm; no rules are built. Known here only from Taatgen 2005.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Second-hand only. I did not find a test that separates the instance account from compilation.
agent_relevance: Open gap: retrieving whole past episodes (as ExpeL does) is the instance route.

source: Taatgen (2013) The nature and transfer of cognitive skills, Psychological Review 120(3) (not opened; PDF not found)
finding: Listed on Taatgen's page as the key paper on transfer of skills. Content not read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Listing only.
agent_relevance: Likely relevant to whether routines transfer across tasks; fetch later.
